newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks to improve ties with European Union.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks to improve ties with European Union.

text.p: President Bill Clinton met with two European Union leaders on Monday seeking closer ties and ways to defuse tensions over a U.S. law punishing foreign firms doing business with Cuba.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, the current president of the EU Council of Ministers, and European Commission President Jacques Santer met in the Oval Office with Clinton for private talks.
"This is an important meeting," said a senior administration official, who said the power of the EU has spread beyond economic and trade issues and into the diplomatic arena as well.
"The European Union is part of the president's strategic approach to Europe," said the official, who was directly involved in the talks.
The official sought to downplay friction between the United States and its European allies, saying "It's sort of natural that there will be disputes."
The most immediate disagreement centres on the so-called "Helms-Burton" law, which punishes firms doing certain types of business with Cuba.

The European Union has threatened to retailiate against American firms if any of its businesses suffer from the law. It was passed in March shortly after four Cuban-American exiles were killed when Cuban MiGs shot down two small U.S. civilian aircraft they were flying off the coast of Cuba.

In addition to expanding the 34-year-old U.S. embargo on Cuba, the law allows lawsuits to be filed in U.S. courts against foreign firms that own or operate properties seized by Cuba from U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before Fidel Castro came to power in 1959.

In July, Clinton ordered the sanctions to come into force, but delayed implementation for six months to calm angry allies in Europe as well as Canada and Mexico. He must decide by mid-January whether the delay should be extended.

The law also allows denial of visas to shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating the seized properties in Cuba. The provision already has been used against officers of a Canadian mining company and a Mexican telecommunications firm.

In a communique following an EU summit in Dublin that ended on Saturday, the leaders scolded Washington, saying it should pursue means against Cuba "other than unilateral action at the expense of closer partners with shared values."

Emphasising Europe's different approach to Cuba, the European Union said it would consider negotiating a trade accord with Havana, making respect for human rights and moves to introduce political reform conditions.
